label: Causal forest pattern
note: Alternative view: a model trained on ADU patterns in Seattle, Austin, Portland and other cities. It puts more ADUs in older, denser places such as Milwaukee County. Same statewide total; only where they land differs.
method: Each place's share is its causal-forest addition for 2027 to 2031 divided by the forest's Wisconsin total. Each year, the adopted central statewide addition is split by those shares, so every year and the five-year total add up to the adopted central figures. Places with no single-family homes get 0. Counties add up their places. Assembly and Senate districts use the same block-based split of each place as the main map. Held-out test (run 3, 5 seeds): median log error for where rates land 0.98 to 0.99 for the forest against 2.27 for our model; for how many permits, the forest was worse (0.253 against 0.218 over the 5 seeds). Check on Milwaukee County: spread by single-family homes alone it would get 1,100 of the 10,492 central permits; the forest gives it 2,428. The forest assumes Milwaukee city would build about 4.0 ADUs per 1,000 single-family homes a year with the law; our model assumes 0.9. In the cities the forest learned from (386 places with 5,000 or more single-family homes and a statewide law), the with-law rate was 0.2 at the 10th percentile, 1.3 at the median and 4.1 at the 90th, so the forest puts Milwaukee near the top. Milwaukee's recent record, 0.09 in 2022 to 2025, was under a ban on ADUs (lifted 2025-08-02), so it says little about the rate with a law. Milwaukee city is outside the forest's training range on housing density and the number of detached homes, so treat this view of Milwaukee with care.

units.rate: additional permits per 1,000 single-family homes per year, 2027 to 2031
